title: Globex x Redwood — Security review (incident response + SLAs)
topics: SOC 2 / incident response program; severity definitions and response times; customer notification and escalation paths; dedicated vs private deployment responsibilities; postmortems and RCAs; audit logging and evidence; shared responsibility model; support vs engineering paging.
summary: Globex security/GRC requested specifics on Redwood’s operational incident handling (Sev definitions, on-call, MTTR targets, communications) and how this differs for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments. Redwood walked through incident declaration, incident command, escalation (Support→SRE/owning team), customer notification expectations, and post-incident RCAs. Globex asked for written artifacts: IR policy excerpt, sample redacted postmortem, and a table of remediation targets by severity/tier suitable for vendor assessment.
questions: Globex: What are your response times by severity (acknowledgement vs mitigate vs full fix)? Do you have 24/7 on-call for hosted and dedicated? How do you notify customers—status page vs direct email—and what is the cadence? Can we get a copy of your incident response policy and a redacted postmortem? For private/VPC deployments, what does Redwood operate vs what’s on us? How do you handle security incidents vs availability incidents?
next_steps: Redwood to send: SOC 2 report under NDA + incident response overview (non-sensitive excerpt) and escalation contacts.
Redwood to send: redacted postmortem sample showing timeline, comms cadence, and action items.
Redwood to send: draft remediation targets table (TTM/TTR) by severity and customer tier for Globex review.
Globex to confirm deployment target (Dedicated vs Private in VPC) and required contractual notification windows.
Schedule follow-up with Globex SRE to review shared responsibility model and monitoring/alerting hooks for private deployments.

transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Globex x Redwood — Security review (incident response + SLAs)
Date: 2025-02-20
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Rachel Kim (Enterprise SLA/Comms), Sean Gallagher (SRE), Dev Patel (Support/CS Escalation)
Globex: Nadia Rahman (Security GRC), Tom Becker (SRE/Platform), Elena Petrova (Procurement), Samir Desai (Eng Manager)

---

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. This is Rachel from Redwood. The goal today is to go through incident response, comms, basically the operational side for security and reliability. Sean from SRE is here, and Dev from Support escalation.

[00:14] Nadia Rahman: Thanks Rachel. Yeah we have our standard vendor review, but also specifically, our leadership asked about response times and escalation for outages. We’ve had bad experiences.

[00:27] Tom Becker: And I’ll ask some nitty gritty questions, sorry in advance.

[00:31] Sean Gallagher: Please do. Better now than during an incident.

[00:36] Rachel Kim: Great. Nadia, do you want to start with the top questions so we can make sure we hit them?

[00:43] Nadia Rahman: Sure. One, do you have 24/7 incident response. Two, how do you define severity levels. Three, what are the response times—like acknowledge, mitigate, permanent fix. Four, how do you notify us—status page, email, phone, Slack. And then, do you have postmortems and can we see an example.

[01:05] Elena Petrova: Also whether any of this can be put into contract language.

[01:10] Rachel Kim: Yep, understood.

[01:12] Sean Gallagher: I can take the operational process, and Rachel can talk comms and contractual mapping.

[01:18] Rachel Kim: Sounds good.

[01:20] Sean Gallagher: Okay. At a high level: for Hosted API and Dedicated pools that we operate, we run 24/7 on-call. There’s an incident commander rotation—SRE IC. We have service owners on-call for major systems: routing/control plane, fleet/capacity, runtime/scheduler, gateway/edge, observability, etc.

[01:41] Tom Becker: When you say 24/7, is it a pager rotation or just “best effort”

[01:46] Sean Gallagher: Pager. We use PagerDuty. It’s a follow-the-sun rotation for primary IC and then US coverage for SMEs; but paging is 24/7.

[01:56] Nadia Rahman: And do you have written incident response policy.

[02:00] Sean Gallagher: Yes. We have an internal incident response process doc and security IR doc. For vendor review we can share a sanitized overview and the SOC 2 controls mapping under NDA.

[02:10] Rachel Kim: We can do that. Some bits are not for broad distribution, but we can provide the core process and escalation contacts.

[02:18] Tom Becker: Can you define severity. Like what’s Sev1.

[02:22] Sean Gallagher: Sure. We have severity definitions aligned to customer impact. Roughly:
- Sev1: widespread customer impact or complete outage of a major surface (e.g., API calls failing across regions, or a dedicated pool hard down).
- Sev2: significant degradation, elevated error rate/latency impacting subset of customers/regions, or partial feature outage like streaming broken.
- Sev3: limited impact, single customer degraded but with workarounds, or internal-only issues.

[02:48] Samir Desai: Do you map that to time targets.

[02:51] Sean Gallagher: Yes. We track time-to-mitigate and time-to-resolve. And then a separate “permanent fix” target depending on severity and category.

[03:00] Nadia Rahman: Category meaning what exactly.

[03:03] Sean Gallagher: Category as in incident type—routing failure, capacity exhaustion, runtime crash, network provider issue, config regression, that kind of thing.

[03:13] Tom Becker: That’s good. We prefer when it’s not just “misc outage.”

[03:18] Rachel Kim: We’re actually standardizing the taxonomy more, because support escalations were ambiguous. So you’ll see in our materials more structured categories.

[03:27] Nadia Rahman: Okay, but can you tell us the actual times. Like, if Sev1, when are you acknowledging and when are you mitigating.

[03:34] Sean Gallagher: Acknowledgement: for Sev1 we target paging acknowledgement within minutes. We generally use a 5 minute acknowledgment target for the on-call to engage, then we’re in an incident channel with an IC.

[03:46] Tom Becker: “Generally” is not a contract.

[03:48] Rachel Kim: Right. So operational targets are different from contractual SLA and notification windows. What we can do is provide standard remediation targets as part of our enterprise support terms, and then the SLA is about availability numbers and credits. But we can absolutely document expected response and escalation.

[04:08] Nadia Rahman: We need something for our vendor packet. It can be “target” but we need it in writing.

[04:12] Rachel Kim: Understood.

[04:14] Sean Gallagher: For mitigation, for Sev1 we aim to begin mitigation immediately—stop the bleeding. Mitigation might be things like routing traffic to a healthy region, falling back to a compatible model variant, disabling a bad feature flag, or capacity rebalancing.

[04:31] Tom Becker: Do you actually have automated fallback.

[04:33] Sean Gallagher: In certain cases, yes. For example if a model version is erroring we can route to the prior pinned version if policy allows. For dedicated it’s a bit more constrained—depends on what you’ve agreed as acceptable fallback.

[04:48] Samir Desai: Our app is fairly sensitive to model changes, so we’d probably opt out.

[04:52] Rachel Kim: That’s common. We can configure fallbacks: no fallback, fallback within same model family, or only within a customer-approved set.

[05:02] Nadia Rahman: And customer communications. How fast do you tell us.

[05:06] Dev Patel: I can take that. For enterprise customers we do multiple channels. There is a public status page for broad incidents, but for dedicated/enterprise we also send direct notifications—usually email to your incident distro, and if we establish it, a shared Slack Connect channel for real-time updates.

[05:24] Elena Petrova: Slack Connect is okay if it’s not the only method.

[05:27] Dev Patel: Not the only. Email is primary for audit trail. During an active Sev1 we’ll post initial notice as soon as we’ve confirmed impact and severity, then a cadence—every 30 minutes is typical, sometimes 15 if it’s very active.

[05:44] Nadia Rahman: So initial notice within what, 30 minutes.

[05:48] Dev Patel: For Sev1, we try to notify quickly. Practically we aim for an initial customer update within 15–30 minutes of declaration, depending on what we know. We don’t want to send “we don’t know anything” but we will say “we’re investigating and here’s current symptoms.”

[06:05] Tom Becker: Who declares. Is it the first engineer who notices.

[06:09] Sean Gallagher: We have alerting that pages SRE and service owners. The first responder can declare, but typically the SRE on-call declares and assumes IC, or assigns an IC. Support can also escalate if customers report issues.

[06:25] Rachel Kim: And we’re formalizing a rule that category and owner are assigned early, so that escalation is clear.

[06:33] Nadia Rahman: That’s good. We’ve seen vendors where it bounces between teams for hours.

[06:38] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, we’re trying to avoid that.

[06:41] Tom Becker: Postmortems—do you do RCAs and do customers get them.

[06:47] Sean Gallagher: For Sev1 and Sev2, yes, we do post-incident reviews. Internal postmortem includes full timeline, contributing factors, action items, and we track completion. For customers, we can share an executive summary and RCA, redacted for sensitive internals. For dedicated enterprise we can do a live incident review call as well.

[07:09] Dev Patel: We also provide a customer-facing summary: impact window, affected surfaces, mitigations applied, and prevention steps.

[07:19] Nadia Rahman: Can we see an example.

[07:21] Sean Gallagher: We can share a redacted sample, yes.

[07:25] Elena Petrova: And evidence. Like audits ask us to show vendor IR.

[07:30] Rachel Kim: That’s where SOC 2 report and the written process overview comes in. We can also provide a letter attesting to our 24/7 on-call and incident management controls.

[07:41] Tom Becker: Okay. Switching to the private deployment question. If we do VPC or on-prem, who’s on the hook.

[07:48] Sean Gallagher: It depends on the operating model. If it’s Redwood Private where we operate day-2, then we still do on-call for the control plane and the runtime components we manage. If it’s fully customer-operated in your environment with only vendor support, then your team is primary responder and we provide escalation support during business hours or per your support package.

[08:10] Nadia Rahman: We’re looking at VPC. Not on-prem right now.

[08:13] Tom Becker: In VPC, do you have access.

[08:16] Sean Gallagher: Access is controlled. Typically it’s customer-managed networking, we use least-privileged access with audit logging. We can operate via a bastion or delegated roles, depending on the setup. We can go deeper later, but for incident response: we can receive telemetry, we can page our on-call, and we can coordinate with your on-call if there’s a network boundary.

[08:37] Nadia Rahman: And security incidents are separate, right.

[08:41] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Security incidents are handled under a dedicated Security IR process with different confidentiality and notification requirements. Operational availability incidents follow the SRE process. That said, we use common metadata like severity, impacted region, customer tier.

[08:57] Tom Becker: Do you have a defined notification window for security incidents.

[09:01] Rachel Kim: We do, but it varies based on the incident type and confirmed impact. We can discuss standard contractual notification terms. Many customers ask for “without undue delay” language plus a maximum window after confirmation. We can align with your requirements, within reason.

[09:20] Elena Petrova: We typically ask for 72 hours after discovery, but I know some vendors push back.

[09:25] Rachel Kim: We’ll take that back to legal. Usually the nuance is “after confirmation of a breach affecting customer data” vs “suspicious activity.”

[09:35] Nadia Rahman: Right.

[09:37] Sean Gallagher: On the reliability side, you asked about response times for mitigate vs fix. We’re in the process of standardizing a table. Today operationally, for a Sev1, the expectation is mitigation quickly—like within an hour or two depending on the category. Permanent fix can be longer, but we track it with deadlines and leadership review.

[09:59] Tom Becker: I want to push: do you have targets by category. Capacity vs routing vs runtime crash are different.

[10:06] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. Routing failures generally can be mitigated fast by policy changes or failover. Capacity exhaustion might require provisioning, which is slower if it’s a cloud capacity constraint, but we can sometimes mitigate with rate limits or moving traffic. Runtime crashes can be quick mitigation if we can roll back a build, but if it’s model-specific it can take longer.

[10:29] Samir Desai: For us, even 20 minutes of 500s is painful.

[10:34] Rachel Kim: Understood. That’s why dedicated capacity is usually paired with stricter operational targets and comms.

[10:41] Tom Becker: Dedicated capacity doesn’t solve routing bugs.

[10:44] Sean Gallagher: Correct. It solves noisy neighbor and capacity contention. Routing/control plane still shared unless you’re on Private with a private control plane.

[10:56] Tom Becker: Good. So if Hosted has an issue, is Dedicated isolated.

[11:01] Sean Gallagher: Often yes for runtime fleet issues, but not always for control plane components, depending on architecture. We can share which components are shared vs isolated in a dedicated deployment.

[11:14] Nadia Rahman: We’ll need that in our assessment. Shared responsibility model basically.

[11:20] Rachel Kim: We can provide a deployment responsibility matrix (RACI-ish) for Hosted, Dedicated, Private.

[11:28] Dev Patel: And from support side, we can define escalation: severity, where to open ticket, when it becomes page to engineering.

[11:37] Tom Becker: Let’s talk escalation. If we see elevated errors, we don’t want to go through generic support for hours.

[11:44] Dev Patel: For enterprise you’ll have a named escalation path. You can open a P1 ticket and that pages the support on-call immediately. Support on-call can page SRE/IC if it meets criteria or if you request it. We can also set up a dedicated “escalation hotline” number depending on package.

[12:03] Nadia Rahman: Criteria means what.

[12:06] Dev Patel: Things like sustained 5xx above threshold, widespread timeouts, or customer critical path. But we also respect customer reported severity. If you say it’s critical, we treat it as such and get IC engaged.

[12:22] Tom Becker: Do you have a single status page.

[12:25] Rachel Kim: Yes, but it’s more general. For dedicated incidents, you’ll get direct comms even if it’s not on public status page.

[12:35] Nadia Rahman: Okay.

[12:38] (crosstalk)

[12:39] Samir Desai: Sorry, one question—do you do blameless postmortems.

[12:42] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Blameless, action-focused.

[12:45] Samir Desai: Do you track action item completion.

[12:48] Sean Gallagher: We do. We track in Linear, with due dates, and SRE reviews overdue items weekly.

[12:57] Tom Becker: That’s good.

[13:00] Nadia Rahman: We also need to know, do you test incident response. Tabletop.

[13:06] Sean Gallagher: We run incident drills occasionally and we do game days for some components. Not monthly for everything, but we do practice.

[13:15] Nadia Rahman: Can you share evidence.

[13:17] Rachel Kim: We can share SOC 2 evidence summaries; raw internal drill logs are usually not shared, but we can provide statements and high-level schedule.

[13:28] Tom Becker: Let’s talk metrics. Do you publish MTTR.

[13:32] Sean Gallagher: Not publicly. Internally we track MTTR and time-to-mitigate. For enterprise QBRs we can share relevant stats, and for your tenancy we can share incident timelines.

[13:45] Nadia Rahman: And do you have SLAs.

[13:47] Rachel Kim: Yes. Availability SLAs for Hosted and Dedicated; Private is more complex depending on operating model. We’ll send the standard SLA language.

[13:58] Elena Petrova: We’ll review.

[14:00] Tom Becker: I’m going to ask about “graceful degradation.” If you have issues, can you degrade rather than hard fail.

[14:08] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Examples: turning off optional features, reducing max context window, limiting concurrency, switching off certain tool-calling paths, and routing to a stable build. We prefer degraded service over outage, but we have to balance correctness.

[14:24] Tom Becker: And do you communicate when you do that.

[14:27] Dev Patel: Yes, we’ll tell you if behavior changes in a customer-impacting way (like reduced context length), especially for dedicated.

[14:35] Nadia Rahman: That’s important.

[14:37] Rachel Kim: Also, your question about written targets: we’re aligning a remediation table—ack, mitigate, permanent fix. It’s not exactly the same as contractual SLA, but it helps operational expectations.

[14:52] Nadia Rahman: We need it.

[14:54] Rachel Kim: We’ll send a draft.

[15:00] Tom Becker: One more: Do you have dependency incident categories. Like if AWS is down.

[15:06] Sean Gallagher: Yes, we track “cloud provider / upstream dependency.” In those cases, mitigation is often failover to a different region/provider if available. For dedicated, depends on where your pool is.

[15:20] Tom Becker: Okay.

[15:22] Nadia Rahman: I’m going to ask a compliance-ish thing: do you keep incident logs. Like who did what.

[15:30] Sean Gallagher: Yes. We keep incident channels, timeline docs, and relevant audit logs. Access is restricted. For security incidents it’s handled separately.

[15:41] Nadia Rahman: And data retention.

[15:44] Rachel Kim: We can share our retention policy. For enterprise we can also configure retention for observability logs to meet your requirements.

[15:55] Elena Petrova: Great.

[16:00] (brief pause)

[16:02] Rachel Kim: Tom, anything else from SRE side.

[16:06] Tom Becker: Maybe we should get clear on escalation. Who is the “single throat to choke” for us.

[16:12] Dev Patel: Support on-call is the front door; for a P1 we engage IC quickly. We can also name an account escalation manager.

[16:22] Rachel Kim: Typically for enterprise, Support on-call + me as the comms / escalation lead, plus SRE IC when there’s an incident.

[16:33] Nadia Rahman: Okay.

[16:35] Samir Desai: Can you do a Slack channel ahead of time.

[16:38] Dev Patel: Yes, we can set up Slack Connect during onboarding.

[16:42] Nadia Rahman: Great.

[16:44] Rachel Kim: We’re at about 17 minutes in the transcript—Fireflies will show this wrong sometimes—but timewise we’re good. I want to make sure we capture action items.

[16:55] Rachel Kim: We will send: (1) incident response overview excerpt + SOC 2 report under NDA, (2) redacted postmortem sample, (3) draft remediation target table by severity and category, and (4) shared responsibility matrix for Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

[17:15] Nadia Rahman: And I’ll send our questionnaire sections and the notification requirement language.

[17:22] Elena Petrova: Yes and contract terms we require.

[17:26] Tom Becker: Can we also do a follow-up technical deep dive on private VPC operations, like what telemetry you get and what you need from us.

[17:34] Sean Gallagher: Yes, happy to.

[17:38] Rachel Kim: Great. We’ll schedule that. Anything else before we drop.

[17:44] Nadia Rahman: No, this was helpful.

[17:46] Tom Becker: Thanks.

[17:48] Dev Patel: Thanks everyone.
